### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue is that when the dissect.cstruct library parses C-style structure definitions that contain field names or structure names that conflict with Python keywords (like `in`), it generates invalid Python code. Specifically, it tries to create class definitions like `class in(Structure):` which causes a `SyntaxError` because `in` is a reserved Python keyword.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Define a structure with a Python keyword as a name (e.g., `in`)
2. Attempt to compile this structure using the cstruct compiler
3. Observe the SyntaxError at compilation time

### 1.5 Best Practices for Fix
- Handle all Python keywords consistently
- Maintain backward compatibility 
- Preserve original names for user-facing APIs
- Make minimal changes to core functionality

## Phase 2. RUNNING: Setting Up and Running Tests

     1	# dissect.cstruct

    53	## Contributing
    54	
    55	The Dissect project encourages any contribution to the codebase. To make your contribution fit into the project, please
    56	refer to [the development guide](https://docs.dissect.tools/en/latest/contributing/developing.html).
    57	
    58	## Usage
    59	All you need to do is instantiate a new cstruct instance and load some structure definitions in there. After that you can start using them from your Python code.
    60	
    61	```python
    62	from dissect import cstruct
    63	
    64	# Default endianness is LE, but can be configured using a kwarg or setting the 'endian' attribute
    65	# e.g. cstruct.cstruct(endian='>') or cparser.endian = '>'
    66	cparser = cstruct.cstruct()
    67	cparser.load("""
    68	#define SOME_CONSTANT   5
    69	
    70	enum Example : uint16 {
    71	    A, B = 0x5, C
    72	};
    73	
    74	struct some_struct {
    75	    uint8   field_1;
    76	    char    field_2[SOME_CONSTANT];
    77	    char    field_3[field_1 & 1 * 5];  // Some random expression to calculate array length
    78	    Example field_4[2];
    79	};
    80	""")
    81	
    82	data = b'\x01helloworld\x00\x00\x06\x00'
    83	result = cparser.some_struct(data)  # Also accepts file-like objects
    84	assert result.field_1 == 0x01
    85	assert result.field_2 == b'hello'
    86	assert result.field_3 == b'world'
    87	assert result.field_4 == [cparser.Example.A, cparser.Example.C]
    88	
    89	assert cparser.Example.A == 0
    90	assert cparser.Example.C == 6
    91	assert cparser.Example(5) == cparser.Example.B
    92	
    93	assert result.dumps() == data
    94	
    95	# You can also instantiate structures from Python by using kwargs
    96	# Note that array sizes are not enforced
    97	instance = cparser.some_struct(field_1=5, field_2='lorem', field_3='ipsum', field_4=[cparser.Example.B, cparser.Example.A])
    98	assert instance.dumps() == b'\x05loremipsum\x05\x00\x00\x00'
    99	```
   100	
   101	By default, all structures are compiled into classes that provide optimised performance. You can disable this by passing a `compiled=False` keyword argument to the `.load()` call. You can also inspect the resulting source code by accessing the source attribute of the structure: `print(cparser.some_struct.source)`.
   102	
   103	More examples can be found in the `examples` directory.
   104	
   105	## Features
   106	### Structure parsing
   107	Write simple C-like structures and use them to parse binary data, as can be seen in the examples.
   108	
   109	### Type parsing
   110	Aside from loading structure definitions, any of the supported types can be used individually for parsing data. For example, the following is all supported:
   111	
   112	```python
   113	from dissect import cstruct
   114	cs = cstruct.cstruct()
   115	# Default endianness is LE, but can be configured using a kwarg or setting the attribute
   116	# e.g. cstruct.cstruct(endian='>') or cs.endian = '>'
   117	assert cs.uint32(b'\x05\x00\x00\x00') == 5
   118	assert cs.uint24[2](b'\x01\x00\x00\x02\x00\x00') == [1, 2]  # You can also parse arrays using list indexing
   119	assert cs.char[None](b'hello world!\x00') == b'hello world!'  # A list index of None means null terminated
   120	```
   121	
   122	### Unions and nested structures
   123	Unions and nested structures are supported, both anonymous and named.
   124	
   125	```python
   126	cdef = """
   127	struct test_union {
   128	    char magic[4];
   129	    union {
   130	        struct {
   131	            uint32 a;
   132	            uint32 b;
   133	        } a;
   134	        struct {
   135	            char   b[8];
   136	        } b;
   137	    } c;
   138	};
   139	
   140	struct test_anonymous {
   141	    char magic[4];
   142	    struct {
   143	        uint32 a;
   144	        uint32 b;
   145	    };
   146	    struct {
   147	        char   c[8];
   148	    };
   149	};
   150	"""
   151	c = cstruct.cstruct()
   152	c.load(cdef)
   153	
   154	assert len(c.test_union) == 12
   155	
   156	a = c.test_union(b'ohaideadbeef')
   157	assert a.magic == b'ohai'
   158	assert a.c.a.a == 0x64616564
   159	assert a.c.a.b == 0x66656562
   160	assert a.c.b.b == b'deadbeef'
   161	
   162	assert a.dumps() == b'ohaideadbeef'
   163	
   164	b = c.test_anonymous(b'ohai\x39\x05\x00\x00\x28\x23\x00\x00deadbeef')
   165	assert b.magic == b'ohai'
   166	assert b.a == 1337
   167	assert b.b == 9000
   168	assert b.c == b'deadbeef'
   169	```
   170	
   171	### Parse bit fields
   172	Bit fields are supported as part of structures. They are properly aligned to their boundaries.
   173	
   174	```python
   175	bitdef = """
   176	struct test {
   177	    uint16  a:1;
   178	    uint16  b:1;  # Read 2 bits from an uint16
   179	    uint32  c;    # The next field is properly aligned
   180	    uint16  d:2;
   181	    uint16  e:3;
   182	};
   183	"""
   184	bitfields = cstruct.cstruct()
   185	bitfields.load(bitdef)
   186	
   187	d = b'\x03\x00\xff\x00\x00\x00\x1f\x00'
   188	a = bitfields.test(d)
   189	
   190	assert a.a == 0b1
   191	assert a.b == 0b1
   192	assert a.c == 0xff
   193	assert a.d == 0b11
   194	assert a.e == 0b111
   195	assert a.dumps() == d
   196	```

   199	The API to access enum members and their values is similar to that of the native Enum type in Python 3. Functionally, it's best comparable to the IntEnum type.

   202	You can implement your own types by subclassing `BaseType` or `RawType`, and adding them to your cstruct instance with `addtype(name, type)`
